description: Important tasks for days 3-7 after a death

tasks.title: Notify Social Security Administration
tasks.description: Report the death to Social Security. If your loved one was receiving benefits, payments must stop. Surviving spouses or dependents may be eligible for survivor benefits.
tasks.why_it_matters: Benefits paid after death must be returned. A surviving spouse may be eligible for survivor benefits, which can be significant—up to 100% of the deceased's benefit amount.
documents_needed: Your Social Security number (if applying for survivor benefits)
tips: The funeral home often reports the death, but verify this was done
Benefits are not prorated—the full month's payment must be returned
Survivor benefits must be applied for—they're not automatic
A surviving spouse can receive benefits as early as age 60 (50 if disabled)

tasks.title: Notify banks and financial institutions
tasks.description: Contact all banks where the deceased had accounts. Joint accounts may need to be retitled. Individual accounts may be frozen until probate is complete.
tasks.why_it_matters: Banks need to freeze accounts to protect the estate. If you're a joint account holder, you need to remove the deceased's name. This also prevents identity theft.
documents_needed: Letters Testamentary or Letters of Administration (for executor access)
tips: Start with banks where you know accounts exist
Check recent mail and email for statements from banks you might not know about
Ask about any automatic payments set up from these accounts
Joint accounts usually transfer automatically to the surviving holder
Safe deposit boxes may require probate court order to access

tasks.title: Notify insurance companies
tasks.description: Contact life insurance companies to file claims. Also notify health, auto, and homeowners insurance companies of the death.
tasks.why_it_matters: Life insurance claims should be filed promptly. Auto and home insurance policies may need to be transferred or cancelled. Health insurance claims may still be pending.
tips: Life insurance claims typically pay within 30-60 days
Check for life insurance through employers, credit cards, and associations
Ask about any accidental death benefits that might apply
Don't cancel auto or home insurance until the property is transferred
COBRA allows dependents to continue health coverage (expensive but important)

tasks.title: Forward or collect mail
tasks.description: Set up mail forwarding from the deceased's address to yours, or arrange to collect mail regularly. This helps you discover accounts and bills you might not know about.
tasks.why_it_matters: Mail reveals accounts, bills, and subscriptions you need to address. Uncollected mail signals an empty home. Some important notices have deadlines.
documents_needed: Death certificate (for some mail forwarding requests)
tips: You can forward mail at usps.com or your local post office
Consider forwarding for 6-12 months to catch everything
Watch for bills, statements, and notices from unknown companies
Some first-class mail won't forward—check the original address periodically
Put a hold on mail during the funeral period if the home will be empty

tasks.title: Notify credit card companies
tasks.description: Contact credit card companies to report the death. Request account closure and final statements. Ask about any life insurance or purchase protection on the cards.
tasks.why_it_matters: Credit card debt is typically paid by the estate, not heirs. Closing accounts prevents fraudulent charges and stops interest from accruing.
tips: You are NOT personally responsible for the deceased's credit card debt (usually)
Ask about any credit card life insurance that might pay off the balance
Request final statements for estate accounting
Cancel any authorized users on the accounts
Watch for recurring charges that indicate subscriptions to cancel

tasks.title: Contact an estate attorney (if needed)
tasks.description: If the estate is complex, involves probate, or there are disputes, consult with an estate attorney. They can guide you through the legal process.
tasks.why_it_matters: An attorney can save time and prevent costly mistakes. Some states have complex probate requirements. If there's no will, an attorney is especially important.
documents_needed: List of assets and their approximate values
tips: Many attorneys offer free initial consultations
Not all estates need to go through probate—an attorney can advise
Ask about flat fees vs. hourly rates vs. percentage of estate
If the deceased had an attorney, start there—they may know the situation
Look for attorneys who specialize in probate/estate law

tasks.title: Gather financial records and statements
tasks.description: Collect recent bank statements, tax returns, investment statements, and other financial documents. These are needed for probate and settling the estate.
tasks.why_it_matters: Financial records reveal the full picture of the estate—assets, debts, and income. The executor needs this information to properly administer the estate.
tips: Look for the last 3 years of tax returns
Gather recent statements from all financial accounts
Check for online accounts—look through email for financial services
Note any recurring income (Social Security, pensions, rental income)
Create a spreadsheet to track all assets and debts discovered

tasks.title: Write and publish obituary
tasks.description: Write an obituary for publication in newspapers and online. This informs the broader community and provides details about memorial services.
tasks.why_it_matters: An obituary notifies friends and acquaintances who might not hear through personal channels. It's also a way to honor your loved one's life and legacy.
tips: Include: full name, age, date of death, survivors, service details
Consider what your loved one would have wanted to be remembered for
Avoid listing specific funeral times if concerned about home security
Many newspapers charge by the word—be aware of costs
Free options include legacy.com and funeral home websites
